items.settingsPath: Nothing to put back: Microsoft ended Mail and Calendar in December 2024. Outlook from the Microsoft Store replaces them.
items.name: Mail and Calendar
items.desc: Discontinued by Microsoft; kept only for legacy accounts.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run, then install Outlook from the Microsoft Store.
symptoms: email link asks for an app
items.name: New Outlook for Windows
items.desc: The web-based mail client Windows preinstalls, and the Windows Update channel and the switch from classic Outlook that put it back. Start may still show an Outlook pin that reinstalls it when clicked, and mail links need another mail app chosen.

items.settingsPath: Install Microsoft Teams from teams.microsoft.com or the Store.
items.name: Microsoft Teams (new client, work and personal)
items.desc: The Teams app, for every account. It is one app for work and personal accounts alike, so a work Teams deployed this way goes too. Not offered on a domain-joined machine.
items.riskNote: If you use Teams for work or school, this removes it. Reinstall it from teams.microsoft.com.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall the Microsoft 365 app from the Store.
items.name: Microsoft 365 hub tile
items.desc: The Office upsell shortcut, not Office itself.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Media Player from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Media Player
items.desc: The built-in music and video player. Legacy Windows Media Player is a separate optional feature and stays.
items.riskNote: It is the default audio and video player. Removing it means music and video files, .mp3 and .mp4 included, have no handler until you set another.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Movies and TV from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Movies and TV
items.desc: Store video playback.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Phone Link from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Phone Link and Cross Device
items.desc: Also removes the Mobile Devices integration.
items.riskNote: Removes phone integration and the Mobile Devices panel in Settings.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall the People app from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: People app
items.desc: The People contacts app. The shell component behind it is an in-box part of Windows and stays.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Get Help from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Get Help
items.riskNote: Windows' own troubleshooters (Settings > System > Troubleshoot) now run inside Get Help, so they stop opening.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run. On builds that still have it, Tips can be reinstalled from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Tips and Get Started
items.desc: The Tips app where a build still has it, and on Enterprise and Education the policy that switches the Get Started experience off. Pro and Home have no switch for Get Started itself.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Sticky Notes from the Microsoft Store. Notes synced to your account come back with it.
items.name: Sticky Notes
items.desc: The desktop notes app.
items.riskNote: People genuinely use this and notes are stored locally. Check nothing is in it first.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Windows Maps from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Windows Maps
items.desc: Plus the MapsBroker service and its update tasks.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Clock from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Clock and Alarms
items.desc: Alarms, timers, world clock, and focus sessions.
items.riskNote: Includes alarms, timers, and focus sessions, not just a clock.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Sound Recorder from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Sound Recorder
items.desc: The built-in voice recorder.
items.riskNote: The default voice recorder. Nothing else in Windows replaces it.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Feedback Hub from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Feedback Hub

items.settingsPath: Nothing to put back on current builds: Windows Mixed Reality was removed in 24H2, and 3D Builder and Print 3D are no longer offered. On older builds, reinstall from the Microsoft Store where they are still listed.
items.name: 3D Builder, Print 3D, and MR Portal
items.desc: All discontinued by Microsoft.

items.settingsPath: Nothing to put back: Microsoft retired Dev Home in 2025 and removed it from Windows, and aka.ms/devhome now opens Settings > System > Advanced instead.
items.name: Dev Home
items.desc: Deprecated by Microsoft.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Microsoft Journal from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Microsoft Journal

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Microsoft To Do from the Store. Your tasks are stored online and come back with it.
items.name: Microsoft To Do
items.desc: Microsoft's task list app.
items.riskNote: Syncs with Outlook tasks. Removing the app does not delete the tasks.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Microsoft Family Safety from the Microsoft Store. The family group and its limits belong to the Microsoft account, so nothing needs setting up again.
items.name: Microsoft Family Safety
items.desc: The app for a Microsoft family group's screen time limits, content filters, and activity reports.
items.riskNote: Anyone managing a family group from this PC loses the app for it. The group and its limits belong to the Microsoft account, so nothing is deleted, and family.microsoft.com still shows and changes them.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Power Automate from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Power Automate Desktop

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Whiteboard from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Whiteboard

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Quick Assist from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Quick Assist
items.desc: Microsoft's built-in remote assistance tool.
items.riskNote: Removes Microsoft remote assistance. Worth removing on machines used by people who might be talked through a scam, but you lose an easy support route.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Camera from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Camera app
items.desc: The built-in camera app.
items.riskNote: Some webcam setups and third-party apps hand off to the Camera app for capture.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Photos from the Microsoft Store, or right-click a picture, Open with, Choose another app.
items.name: Photos app
items.desc: The built-in photo viewer and editor.
items.riskNote: The default image viewer. Image files will have no handler until you set another.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Paint from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Paint
items.desc: The in-box image editor.
items.riskNote: Nothing else opens .bmp files by default, and Edit with Paint leaves the image right-click menu. Reinstallable from the Store at any time.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Notepad from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Notepad
items.desc: The in-box plain text editor.
items.riskNote: Double-clicking a .txt, .log, or .ini file may ask which app to use until you choose one. The classic notepad.exe stays wherever Windows still has its optional Notepad (system) feature, so software that opens a readme by handing the path to notepad.exe keeps working there.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Calculator from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Calculator
items.desc: The in-box calculator.
items.riskNote: The calculator key on keyboards that have one stops doing anything, and so does typing a sum into Start.

items.settingsPath: Reinstall Snipping Tool from the Microsoft Store.
items.name: Snipping Tool
items.desc: The in-box screenshot and screen recording tool.
items.riskNote: Win+Shift+S and the Print Screen key's snipping overlay stop working - they are handled by this app rather than by the shell - and so does screen recording. Win+Print Screen still saves a full-screen capture to Pictures\Screenshots.

items.settingsPath: Run wsreset -i from an administrator prompt and wait a few minutes: it downloads and reinstalls the Store. Undoing the run cannot put it back, because the package is removed for every account.
items.name: Microsoft Store
items.desc: The Microsoft Store client.
items.riskNote: Without the Store you cannot install or update Store apps - and every other app this toolkit removes gives the Store as its way back, so that route goes too until the Store is reinstalled with wsreset -i.

items.settingsPath: Undo the run, which turns Edge's updater back on, then reinstall Microsoft Edge from microsoft.com/edge.
symptoms: you will need an app to open this
items.name: Uninstall Microsoft Edge
items.desc: Uninstalls the Edge browser, and once it is gone switches off its updater and the Windows Update channel that reinstalls it. If Windows refuses the uninstall, Edge is left exactly as it was, still updating. WebView2 Runtime is kept.
items.riskNote: Edge's updater is also what keeps WebView2 Runtime patched, so once Edge is really gone and the updater is off, WebView2 - which other programs use to show web pages - stops getting security updates. Undoing the run turns the updater back on. If a replacement browser was picked and did not install, Edge is kept rather than leaving the machine with no browser.

Windows decides whether Edge may be uninstalled at all: outside about thirty-five EEA regions the answer is no, so this run sets your home region to Ireland just long enough to run the uninstaller and sets it back immediately (also written to the rollback script in case the run is interrupted between the two; your language, keyboard, and formats are untouched). Current builds can still refuse, because they also check which program asked and accept Settings; when that happens nothing else is changed and the item says so. When it does uninstall, the updater it shares with WebView2 goes off, so WebView2 - which apps that embed a browser use - stops receiving security updates until Edge or the updater is reinstalled. A few Windows surfaces expect Edge and may fall back awkwardly.
